newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilian leader's "Silent Revolution" moves on.
newsitem.headline: Brazilian leader's "Silent Revolution" moves on.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Tuesday took another step forward in his "Silent Revolution", winning a first vote in Congress on a bill that will allow him to stand again in 1998.
The vote by the Chamber of Deputies in favour of changing the constitution was probably the biggest gambling victory yet for the poker-loving Brazilian leader.

It may also mark a watershed in his two-year-old administration. Political analysts predict the right to stand for a second term will give the popular president extra clout in pushing key economic reforms through Congress.
Cardoso saw the vote as an endorsement of his rule though the bill must be approved again by the lower house and passed by the Senate twice before it takes effect.
"He sees it as a decision to carry on the policy of economic stability," presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral told reporters.
Victory in the first re-election vote seemed an uncertain bet only last week. But feverish negotiations by Cardoso's allies appeared to have won many waverers to his side.
During the 1994 presidential campaign, Cardoso was reported to have told a political adviser: "I never take on anything unless I know I can win."
Since then he has developed a reputation as a charmer who does not hesitate to take off the gloves when things get rough.
"The president told them (rebel deputies) in very clear terms that he wanted them to vote this week and that did it," an official said.

A 65-year-old leftist sociologist turned liberal free-marketeer, Cardoso took office in January 1995 after voters overwhelmingly endorsed an inflation-busting plan he had introduced as finance minister.
His 30-month Real Plan reform programme brought inflation down from 5,000 percent a year to just 10 percent in 1996 and helped lift some 13 million Brazilians above the poverty line.
Cardoso was born in Rio de Janeiro into a military family, educated at Sao Paulo university and trained as a sociologist.
Several of the two dozen books he has written on Latin America are standard university text books.
During Brazil's 1964-85 military governments, Cardoso the professor fled into exile, living in France and Chile.

As president, he has vowed to bring order to the country's tangled finances, open it up to trade and reduce the enormous gap between rich and poor. He has also championed a new approach to human rights, trying to eliminate widespread child and slave labour.
But essential tax, civil service and pensions reforms have become bogged down in Congress.

Cardoso maintains the country is on the mend despite criticisms he has failed to improve wealth distribution in Brazil, identified by the United Nations as one of the most unfair in the world. He says another term is essential if his economic reforms are to prosper.
"Out there, a silent revolution is taking place," he said in a recent speech, adding that the poor were buying television sets and refrigerators for the first time in their lives.
